Let me carefully review this proposed solution to IMO 2026 Problem 1.

The problem: 2026 integers greater than 1 on a blackboard. A move: choose two integers m>1, n>1 from different places, replace them with gcd(m,n) and lcm(m,n)/gcd(m,n). Continue while possible.

Part 1: Prove that after finitely many moves, exactly one integer M on the board is greater than 1.
Part 2: Prove M doesn't depend on the choices.

Proposed solution:

Termination: define P = product of all entries, K = number of entries > 1. Order (P, K) lexicographically.

A move on m, n > 1: new entries g = gcd(m,n) and lcm(m,n)/g. Product of the two new entries is g · lcm/g = lcm = mn/g. So the new product P' = P/g.

- If g > 1, P' < P (strictly, since g ≥ 2).
- If g = 1, new entries are 1 and mn, so P' = P, and the two nonunits m, n (both > 1) are replaced by 1 and mn — wait, but mn > 1, so the count K: we had two entries > 1 replaced by one entry > 1 (mn) and one 1. So K decreases by 1.

Hence (P, K) strictly decreases lexicographically after every move. Since P is a positive integer bounded below by 1, it can only strictly decrease finitely many times; between decreases K decreases, and K ≤ 2026 bounded below by... well K ≥ 0, so each "block" of moves with fixed P has at most finitely many moves. Total moves finite. Good.

Wait — actually, I need to double-check the claim "if g = 1, the new entries are 1 and mn". Indeed with g = 1, gcd = 1 and lcm(m,n)/1 = lcm(m,n) = mn (since coprime). Yes.

Also, if g > 1, P strictly decreases: P' = P/g < P since g ≥ 2 and P > 0. Yes.

One subtlety: in the case g > 1, does the lexicographic order strictly decrease? (P, K) → (P', K') with P' < P, so yes regardless of K'. Good.

Termination is fine. This is a standard argument.

When the process stops: at most one entry > 1 (otherwise another legal move exists). Also, a legal move never removes all nonunits: if g > 1, first output g > 1; if g = 1, second output mn > 1. So at least one nonunit remains at each stage. Initially all 2026 entries > 1, so K ≥ 1 always. Hence terminal board has exactly one nonunit M. Good.

Wait, but there's a subtle point: the process "continues to make moves while it is possible to do so" — the problem says he continues while possible. Termination says any maximal sequence is finite, and at termination exactly one entry > 1. That's what part 1 asks: "regardless of the choices, after finitely many moves, exactly one integer M on the blackboard is greater than 1." Good.

Part 2: value of M forced.

Fix prime p. Track exponent vector (e_1, ..., e_2026) where e_i = v_p(x_i). A move on entries with exponents a, b replaces them with min(a,b) and |a−b| (since v_p(lcm/gcd) = max − min = |a−b|). Wait: v_p(lcm(m,n)) = max(a,b), v_p(gcd(m,n)) = min(a,b). So v_p(lcm/gcd) = max(a,b) − min(a,b) = |a−b|. Yes.

The gcd of the multiset {e_i} is invariant: replacing (a,b) by (min(a,b), |a−b|). gcd(a,b) = gcd(a, b−a) = gcd(min, |a−b|). Standard Euclidean identity. Since the gcd of the full list is gcd(gcd of pair, gcd of rest), and the pair's gcd is preserved, the total gcd G_p is invariant. Good.

At terminal board, the exponent list is (v_p(M), 0, ..., 0), and gcd(c, 0, ..., 0) = c. So v_p(M) = G_p = gcd(v_p(A_1), ..., v_p(A_2026)). This holds for all primes p. Only finitely many primes divide any A_i, and a prime absent initially has all-zero exponents, which stays all-zero forever (moves only produce min and |a−b| of existing exponents, so zeros stay zeros — indeed if all e_i = 0 for prime p, then min = 0 and |a−b| = 0, so it remains all zeros; the invariant also gives G_p = 0 so v_p(M) = 0). Hence M = ∏_p p^{gcd of valuations}, finite product. Good.

So the final M equals the product over primes of p^{g_p} where g_p = gcd of p-adic valuations of initial entries. Note: this is the largest integer d such that... hmm, actually M = product p^{gcd(e_i)}. Interesting. For example with entries 4 and 8: v_2 = (2,3), gcd = 1, so M = 2.
